findings.title: Promise within a reciprocal covenant frame
findings.claim: Within the declared pericope, the promise in 5:9 is colored by the opening command to fulfill binding contracts: the believing recipients appear within a reciprocal covenant frame in which their own commitments are also made whole.
findings.mechanism: The focus promise occurrence at 5:9 meets the completion and binding-contract occurrences at 5:1. Their contact changes the promise from an isolated divine assurance into a promise heard within a field where human commitments are also required to become reliable.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see why the promise follows a scene of human promise-keeping: the recipients are characterized by a response that has covenantal shape, not only by a status that receives an outcome.
findings.containment: The recoverable primary remains God's promise of forgiveness and a great reward. This is an attributed pericope-level coloring, not a claim that 5:9 states a bilateral contract with God; 5:1 may also function as a legal preface rather than an exhaustive account of the focus's logic.

epistemic.reason: Every cited anchor has exact Arabic and matching HFT coordinates, but the reader identity is legacy_unbound, context morphology is not supplied, and the reciprocal arrow is an attributed synthesis of the supplied role evidence.

findings.title: Rectifying deeds under hostility
findings.claim: The pericope colors the rectifying deeds in 5:9 with public practices that keep hatred from reproducing corruption: cooperation in good, fair witness, measured judgment, and repeated justice under enmity.
findings.mechanism: The focus deed occurrence meets the repeated 5:2 and 5:8 sequence in which hostility is followed by a prohibition of excess or injustice and a commanded counterpractice. The contact gives the open phrase 'rectifying deeds' a public and relational field without exhausting it.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the deeds as actions that repair a damaged social field, especially where grievance would otherwise bend judgment, rather than as an unbounded list of private merit.
findings.containment: The primary phrase still names the good and rectifying deeds of the believing group. The hostility tests, cooperation, equity, and justice are attributed diagnostics and prominent examples, not an exhaustive definition; unresolved context roots remain without invented glosses.

epistemic.reason: Exact Arabic anchors and word coordinates are supplied for 5:2, 5:8, and 5:9, while the contextual morphology and non-focus branch records are unresolved and the selection of these practices as diagnostics remains attributed HFT inference.

findings.title: Reward whose yield can collapse
findings.claim: The promised reward in 5:9 is colored as an owed return linked to performed work, while the neighboring 5:5 sequence makes that yield contingent on enacted faith: the return has covenantal answerability without becoming mechanically banked.
findings.mechanism: The focus reward occurrence meets the concrete contractual due in 5:5 and the same ayah's sequence joining faith, rejection, work, collapse, and final loss. This changes the reader's model of reward from an automatically secured unit to a return whose endurance is tied to the enacted side of faith.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold together the familiar language of compensation and the neighboring warning about collapsed work, seeing why the promise has the feel of a due while retaining a live condition on its yield.
findings.containment: The primary remains the promise of a great reward to the defined believing group. The 5:5 payment is not equated with the eschatological promise, and the adjacent contrary outcome remains a boundary; the supplied HFT inference may be replaced by a reading that keeps the legal payment and final-loss uses distinct.

epistemic.reason: The 5:5 and 5:9 Arabic surfaces and HFT coordinates are supplied, with independent focus lexicon facets for reward, faith, and work; the cross-use synthesis and its conditional implication remain attributed under legacy_unbound provenance.

findings.title: Forgiveness as protective accommodation
findings.claim: The promised forgiveness in 5:9 is colored by the pericope's accommodation logic: it protects people under constraint and non-willful intent, removes crushing burden, and restores a whole rectifying relation.
findings.mechanism: The focus forgiveness occurrence meets 5:3's necessity, hunger, intent, mercy, and forgiveness sequence and 5:6's alternate purification, rejected hardship, and completion sequence. Their contact changes forgiveness from post hoc concealment alone into a protective governance that keeps constrained agents within restoration.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the promised forgiveness as an active protection that reads bodily constraint and intention, then preserves restoration and completion, rather than as a bare cancellation after failure.
findings.containment: The primary remains the promised forgiveness granted to the believing group who perform rectifying work. The protective economy is an attributed synthesis across 5:3 and 5:6; legal accommodation and eschatological forgiveness may remain parallel mechanisms, and the relation is not a complete definition of forgiveness.

epistemic.reason: Exact Arabic anchors and HFT coordinates are supplied for 5:3, 5:6, and 5:9, while context morphology and several context-only branch records are unresolved and the single protective logic is explicitly an attributed synthesis.
